title: Paginated List
story: Your app has 10,000 search results. You can't show them all on one screen — users would scroll forever. Instead, you need pages: results 1-20 on page 1, results 21-40 on page 2, and so on. Welcome to pagination — every website and app uses it.
why: Pagination is how every data-heavy application — search engines, social feeds, product listings — breaks large datasets into consumable chunks, and it's built on simple Vec slicing logic.
analogy: Pagination is like a book — you don't read the entire book at once. You flip to page N, and each page has a fixed number of lines (page size). The `get_page` function IS the act of turning to a specific page.
try_it: Change page size to 2 and re-run — notice how the number of pages changes. Then write `paginate_with_info` that returns a struct containing the page items, current page number, total pages, and whether there's a next/previous page. Add a `paginate_map_keys` function that paginates through a Map's keys (given a Vec of keys).
tips: Page numbers are 0-indexed: page 0 = items 0 to page_size-1, page 1 = items page_size to 2*page_size-1
Always clamp `end` to `items.len()` — the last page is often shorter than page_size
Generic `[T]` means this works with any Vec type — one function, infinite reusability
common_mistakes: 1-indexing pages — `page * page_size` assumes page 0 is the first page; if page 1 is first, use `(page-1) * page_size`
Forgetting to check `start >= total` — requesting page 100 of a 10-item list returns an empty Vec
Using `items.len()` for end without clamping — accessing `items[actual_end]` past the vector bounds
